page_01: Ladybirds can eat thousands of tiny aphids in their lifetime!
page_02: A ladybird's bright spots tell birds: I taste yucky!
page_03: A honeybee can visit up to 100 flowers on one trip!
page_04: Honeybees do a waggle dance to show friends where flowers are.
page_05: Each honeybee hive has one queen bee who lays all the eggs.
page_06: Butterflies taste their food with their feet!
page_07: A caterpillar sheds its skin about five times as it grows.
page_08: Inside a chrysalis, a caterpillar turns into a butterfly.
page_09: The bright blue Ulysses butterfly lives in tropical Queensland.
page_10: Emperor gum moth caterpillars munch on gum leaves all day.
page_11: An ant can carry many times its own body weight!
page_12: Ants live together in nests with lots of busy rooms.
page_13: Bull ants are Aussie ants with big eyes and big jaws.
page_14: Dragonflies can fly forwards, backwards and even hover!
page_15: Fireflies make their own light to talk to their friends.
page_16: Glow-worms light up Australian caves like tiny stars.
page_17: Christmas beetles come out in the Aussie summer, near Christmas!
page_18: Rainbow stag beetles shine green, gold and purple.
page_19: Dung beetles roll balls of poo bigger than themselves!
page_20: Jewel beetles shine like little gemstones in the sun.
page_21: A weevil is a beetle with a long nose called a snout.
page_22: Grasshoppers hear with ears on their tummies!
page_23: Crickets sing by rubbing their wings together.
page_24: Katydids look just like leaves, so birds can't spot them.
page_25: Green grocer cicadas are some of the loudest insects on Earth.
page_26: A praying mantis can turn its head to look over its shoulder.
page_27: Stick insects hide by looking just like twigs.
page_28: A snail carries its shell home everywhere it goes.
page_29: Snails glide along on a slippery trail of slime.
page_30: Earthworms have no eyes, but they can sense light.
page_31: Australia's giant Gippsland earthworm can grow over a metre long!
page_32: Spiders are not insects. They have eight legs!
page_33: Spider silk is stronger than steel of the same thickness.
page_34: Huntsman spiders are big and fast, and love hiding under bark.
page_35: Tiny peacock spiders dance and wave their bright fans.
page_36: Blue-banded bees are Aussie bees with bright blue stripes.
page_37: Some Australian native bees have no sting at all!
page_38: Leaf-cutter bees cut round pieces of leaf to build their nests.
page_39: Most moths fly at night and have fluffy, feathery antennae.
page_40: Bogong moths fly hundreds of kilometres to cool mountain caves.
page_41: Termites build giant mud mounds in Australia's north.
page_42: Centipede means 100 legs, but no centipede has exactly 100!
page_43: Millipedes have two pairs of legs on most body parts.
page_44: Slaters roll into a tight ball when they feel scared.
page_45: Water striders can walk on top of the water!
page_46: Mud dauber wasps build nests out of tiny balls of mud.
page_47: Giant burrowing cockroaches can live for about ten years!
page_48: Lacewings have see-through wings that look like lace.
page_49: Every insect has six legs and three body parts.
page_50: Thanks for exploring the wonderful world of minibeasts!
